title: The return of the high street
text: The obituary of the high street has been written {{1}} times, and for understandable reasons. Out-of-town retail parks and then online giants {{2}} a heavy toll: bank branches, butchers and bookshops closed in waves, and vacancy rates {{3}} past twenty per cent in some towns. Yet predictions of total collapse proved {{4}} exaggerated. What has come back is not what left. In their {{5}} have arrived coffee shops, barbers, nail bars and small galleries; hospitality now {{6}} for nearly half of all new lettings on British high streets. The change reflects a deeper logic rather than sentiment. Anything that fits through a letterbox has largely migrated online, so the survivors trade in {{7}} that will not post: haircuts, hot bread, coffee in company, an hour of trying things on with a friend. Councils have adjusted their thinking too — less parking enforcement and more market stalls, less retail planning and more housing above the shops. Obituary writers will no doubt be busy again; the high street, meanwhile, keeps {{8}} back in whatever shape the decade demands.

gaps.explanation: 'has been written countless times' — adjective before a noun.
'took a heavy toll' — fixed collocation for causing damage.
'vacancy rates climbed past twenty per cent' — rise intransitively.
'proved prematurely exaggerated' — exaggerated before the fact.
'In their place have arrived' — fixed phrase: as replacements.
'hospitality accounts for half of lettings' — makes up that share.
'trade in experiences that will not post' — activities, not objects.
